title: System design in a nutshell
lede: Every component solves one problem and brings new ones: cost, complexity and new ways to fail. Designing a system means choosing which problems are worth having, and when.

sections.heading: Why think about it at all

items.text: A system is the set of parts that serve your users. Its design decides where work happens, where data lives, and what happens when something breaks.
A few decisions are expensive to change later: how data is modelled, who owns it, how it is secured. Those deserve thought early.
Most decisions can wait. Building for problems you don't have costs the time you need to find users.

items.title: Before building:
items.text: just enough to choose a simple start and avoid the decisions that are hard to undo.

items.title: When a signal appears:
items.text: pages slow down, outages hurt, the bill grows, or teams block each other.

items.title: Before a known event:
items.text: a launch, a campaign, a large customer.

items.title: Not because a big company does it.
items.text: Their problems come from a scale you may never reach.

sections.heading: Put the constraints on the table

items.title: Users:
items.text: how many, where, and at what times? Design for the peak, not the average.

items.title: Workload:
items.text: mostly reads or writes? How much data, and how fast does it grow?

items.title: Speed:
items.text: what must answer instantly, and what can happen later?

items.title: Correctness:
items.text: which data must never be wrong or lost (money), and which can be a little stale (a feed)?

items.title: Availability:
items.text: what does an hour of downtime cost?

items.title: Budget and team:
items.text: money, people, skills and time to deliver.

items.title: Rules:
items.text: privacy, regulation, where data may be stored.

sections.heading: Before adding a component, ask in order

items.title: What is the problem, exactly?
items.text: Name the symptom and measure it. No number, no problem.

items.title: Can what we have solve it?
items.text: An index, a better query, a bigger machine, a setting.

items.title: What is the simplest thing that would?
items.text: Prefer managed services and well-known tools.

items.title: What does it cost?
items.text: Money, running it, learning it, and new ways to fail.

items.title: What happens when it fails?
items.text: If everything stops, it is a new single point of failure.

items.title: What does it do to the data?
items.text: Copies can be out of date. Which one is the source of truth?

items.title: Can we undo it?
items.text: Move fast on reversible choices; slow down on one-way doors.

items.title: How will we know it worked?
items.text: Compare the number from step 1, before and after.

sections.heading: Common signals and the usual first answer

map.answer: A bigger machine, then copies behind a load balancer
Spares in another zone, automatic failover

map.signal: The database is the slow part
map.answer: Indexes, then a cache, then read replicas
Clear modules, then a few services

items.title: Speed or freshness:
items.text: copies such as caches and replicas are fast but can be out of date.

items.title: Simple or scalable:
items.text: every new part is one more thing to run, watch and fix.

items.title: Cost or uptime:
items.text: redundancy roughly doubles the cost of what it protects.

items.title: Now or later:
items.text: plan for ten times today's load, not a thousand.
